HARD_FRAGMENTS.fact: Created by Urban Müller in 1993 to make the smallest possible compiler. Only > < + - . , [ ] are commands — this fragment is the printing half of the program.

HARD_FRAGMENTS.fact: Ook! (David Morgan-Mar) re-encodes Brainfuck for orangutans — a nod to Terry Pratchett’s Librarian. Pairs of Ook./Ook?/Ook! make the eight commands.

HARD_FRAGMENTS.fact: COW (Sean Heber, 2003) has 12 instructions — MoO, mOo, MOO, mOO, MMM and friends. Under the hide, it is Brainfuck-like, with MOO/moo as its loop.

HARD_FRAGMENTS.fact: In the Shakespeare Programming Language (2001), characters are variables and nouns carry values — “hero” is positive, “coward” is negative — so an insult literally computes. “Speak your mind!” prints.

HARD_FRAGMENTS.note: // Tiny excerpt (1–2 lines) — a corner of the grid, mid-execution. The pointer is not moving left-to-right any more.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.weakHint: Don’t assume it reads left to right.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.fact: Befunge-93 (Chris Pressey, 1993) runs on a 2D grid: > < ^ v steer the instruction pointer, _ and | are conditional turns, and @ ends the program. It can rewrite its own grid as it runs.

HARD_FRAGMENTS.note: // Tiny excerpt (truncated) — an ordered list like this, plus a starting number, is a complete program in this language. The rest of the list has been cut.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.weakHint: There is almost nothing here except numbers and one repeated separator.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.fact: Fractran (John Conway) is Turing complete with nothing but a list of fractions: multiply the current number by the first fraction that gives an integer, and repeat. Its most famous list generates prime numbers.

HARD_FRAGMENTS.note: // Tiny excerpt (1–2 lines) — backticks and single letters. There are no variables, no numbers and no keywords hiding anywhere else in the language.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.weakHint: Two kinds of marks do almost everything here.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.fact: Unlambda (David Madore) is functional programming stripped to combinators — `k, `s and `i — plus .x, which prints the character x. It was designed to make functional programming feel as awkward as Brainfuck makes imperative programming feel.

HARD_FRAGMENTS.code:
Blub. Blub. Blub! Blub?
Blub? Blub. Blub. Blub?
HARD_FRAGMENTS.note: // Tiny excerpt (1–2 lines) — one word, repeated. Whether it ends in . ? or ! is the entire instruction set.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.weakHint: One word keeps returning — and it belongs underwater.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.fact: Blub re-encodes Brainfuck the way Ook! does for orangutans — but for fish. Blub. Blub? and Blub! pair up into the same eight tape commands.

HARD_FRAGMENTS.note: // Tiny excerpt (1–2 lines) — the PLEASEs have been cut from this stretch. In the full program they are load-bearing: too few is rude, too many is grovelling.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.weakHint: Something polite is conspicuously missing from this stretch.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.fact: INTERCAL (1972) is the original parody language, by Don Woods and Jim Lyon. DO and PLEASE DO are interchangeable to the parser — except the compiler counts your PLEASEs and rejects you for rudeness or for excessive politeness.

HARD_FRAGMENTS.note: // Tiny excerpt (1–2 lines) — after each instruction, the code encrypts itself, so the same character never means the same thing twice.

HARD_FRAGMENTS.fact: Malbolge (Ben Olmstead, 1998) encrypts its own code after every instruction. Nobody wrote a working program in it for two years — the first Hello World was found by a search algorithm, not a human.

HARD_FRAGMENTS.note: // Tiny excerpt (1–2 lines) — only six distinct characters appear in this entire language, and this fragment uses all of them.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.weakHint: Only a handful of characters, yet it’s a dialect of something everyday.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.fact: JSFuck writes any JavaScript using only []()!+ : brackets and coercion between booleans, strings and numbers spell out letters. It runs in any browser console.

l o ; W o

HARD_FRAGMENTS.fact: Hexagony (Martin Ender) runs on a hexagonal grid — the source code itself forms a hexagon of characters, and the instruction pointer moves in six directions, wrapping around the edges.

HARD_FRAGMENTS.note: // Tiny excerpt (1–2 lines) — the tail of a one-line program and the row beneath it. The pointer wraps around the tank’s edges and works off a stack.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.weakHint: The layout wraps — what leaves one edge comes back elsewhere.

Say your heart

HARD_FRAGMENTS.note: // Tiny excerpt (1–2 lines) — the 🏁 entry point has been cut. What remains is a block, and every keyword inside it is a picture.

HARD_FRAGMENTS.fact: Emojicode is a real, open-source, high-level language — it has classes, generics and closures, all spelled in emoji. 🏁 is the entry point and 😀 is its print.

HARD_FRAGMENTS.note: // Tiny excerpt (1–2 lines) — in this language that is nearly the whole program: a string, then the one symbol that prints it.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.weakHint: Almost everything on show is the message itself — the language is the symbol left over.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.fact: FALSE (Wouter van Oortmerssen, 1993) is a tiny stack language: strings push themselves, and ß pops and prints. It directly inspired GolfScript.

HARD_FRAGMENTS.note: // Tiny excerpt (1–2 lines) — a mid-print slice. The alphabet here has five characters, and one of them is an asterisk.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.weakHint: Same tape, fewer letters — and one of them is a star.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.fact: Smallfuck shrinks Brainfuck to a 5-command bit-tape language (* flips a bit, > and < move, [ ] loop). Whole programs look like a spilled box of asterisks.

HARD_FRAGMENTS.note: // Tiny excerpt (1–2 lines) — mid-print. Familiar-looking commands, but the cells underneath hold one bit each.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.weakHint: It walks like Brainfuck, but each cell can only say yes or no.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.fact: Brainbool is Brainfuck restricted to bit cells: values are built by counting, not stored, which is why its programs are all pointer moves, pluses and dots.

HARD_FRAGMENTS.note: // Tiny excerpt (1–2 lines) — the whole program fits the slice. Execution enters at one symbol and bounces around the grid.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.weakHint: Follow the line, not the reading order — something in here acts like a mirror.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.fact: SNUSP runs like a light beam entering at $ and reflecting off / and \ mirrors; the traced path through the grid is the execution order.

HARD_FRAGMENTS.note: // Tiny excerpt (1–2 lines) — one rule from the program, plus the seed string it starts from has been cut.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.weakHint: There is a before and an after here, separated by a very distinctive sign.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.fact: Thue (John Colagioia, 2000) is pure find-and-replace: rules of the form a::=b rewrite a starting string, and ~ marks text as output instead of a replacement.

HARD_FRAGMENTS.note: // Tiny excerpt (1–2 lines) — slashes are the only punctuation this language has; a pattern, a replacement, and the text it works on.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.weakHint: Count the dividers — the whole grammar fits between them.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.fact: /// (pronounced "slashes") has one construct: /pattern/replacement/ applied to the text that follows, repeatedly. Its Hello World is a single substitution that expands a marker into the greeting.

HARD_WIDE.note: // That is the whole program — one line. This language was built so that source code reads like 1980s rock ballad lyrics.
HARD_WIDE.weakHint: Try singing it. The performance is part of the puzzle.
HARD_WIDE.fact: Rockstar (Dylan Beattie, 2018) makes programs read as song lyrics: “Say” prints, and a line like “Midnight takes your heart and your soul” defines a function with two arguments.

HARD_WIDE.note: // Tiny excerpt (1–2 lines) — only six distinct characters appear in this entire language, and this fragment uses all of them.
HARD_WIDE.weakHint: Only a handful of characters, yet it’s a dialect of something everyday.
HARD_WIDE.fact: JSFuck writes any JavaScript using only []()!+ : brackets and coercion between booleans, strings and numbers spell out letters. It runs in any browser console — a party trick and a security headache in one.

HARD_WIDE.code:
Blub. Blub? Blub. Blub. Blub. Blub. Blub. Blub.
Blub. Blub. Blub! Blub? Blub? Blub. Blub. Blub?
Blub. Blub. Blub. Blub. Blub. Blub. Blub. Blub.
HARD_WIDE.note: // One word, repeated. Whether it ends in . ? or ! is the entire instruction set — the aquatic counterpart of another language in this quiz.
HARD_WIDE.weakHint: One word keeps returning — and it belongs underwater.
HARD_WIDE.fact: Blub re-encodes Brainfuck the way Ook! does for orangutans — but for fish. Blub. Blub? and Blub! pair up into the same eight tape commands.

HARD_WIDE.note: // The original tape language, in full. Eight options below — tap the right one.
HARD_WIDE.weakHint: No words, no letters that mean anything — just eight punctuation marks and a lot of them.
HARD_WIDE.fact: Brainfuck (Urban Müller, 1993) has eight commands — > < + - . , [ ] — and everything else in the file is a comment. The other word-languages in this list are all re-encodings of it.

HARD_WIDE.code:
Ook. Ook? Ook. Ook. Ook. Ook. Ook. Ook. Ook. Ook.
Ook. Ook. Ook. Ook. Ook. Ook. Ook. Ook. Ook. Ook.
Ook? Ook? Ook! Ook? Ook? Ook. Ook. Ook. Ook. Ook?
Ook. Ook. Ook. Ook. Ook. Ook. Ook. Ook. Ook. Ook?
HARD_WIDE.note: // One word, three endings. Pairs of them spell out another language's commands — eight options below.
HARD_WIDE.weakHint: The vocabulary has one word; the punctuation after it does all the talking, in pairs.
HARD_WIDE.fact: Ook! re-encodes Brainfuck for orangutans: the pairs Ook. Ook?, Ook? Ook. and so on map one-to-one onto Brainfuck's eight commands. It was designed by David Morgan-Mar, of Piet fame.

HARD_WIDE.code:
Hello World Souffle.

Ingredients.
72 g haricot beans
101 eggs
108 g lard
111 cups oil
32 zucchinis
119 ml water
114 g red salmon
100 g dijon mustard
33 potatoes

Method.
Put haricot beans into the mixing bowl.
Put eggs into the mixing bowl.
Put lard into the mixing bowl.
Put oil into the mixing bowl.
…
HARD_WIDE.note: // A complete recipe that is also a complete program — the ingredients are data. Eight options below.
HARD_WIDE.weakHint: Read the units: grams, cups, and a method. The kitchen is not a metaphor here.
HARD_WIDE.fact: Chef (David Morgan-Mar) programs are recipes: ingredient quantities are input data, mixing bowls are stacks, and baking dishes are output. A good Chef program should ideally be cookable, too.

HARD_WIDE.code:
The Infamous Hello World Program.

Romeo, a young man with a remarkable patience.
Juliet, a likewise young woman of remarkable grace.
Hamlet, the flatterer of Andersen Insulting A/S.

        Act I: Hamlet's insults and flattery.

        Scene I: The insulting of Romeo.

[Enter Hamlet and Romeo]

Hamlet:
 You lying stupid fatherless big smelly half-witted coward!
 You are as stupid as the difference between a handsome
 rich brave hero and thyself! Speak your mind!
HARD_WIDE.note: // A play script that is also a program — characters are variables, and their lines are arithmetic. Eight options below.
HARD_WIDE.weakHint: Dramatis personae, acts and scenes: the insults are doing arithmetic in disguise.
HARD_WIDE.fact: In the Shakespeare Programming Language (Kalle Hasselström & Jon Åslund, 2001), characters are stacks, entering and exiting the stage selects them, and a line like "You are as stupid as the difference…" is an assignment. Output happens one spoken character at a time.

HARD_WIDE.code:
IT'S SHOWTIME
TALK TO THE HAND "HELLO WORLD"
YOU HAVE BEEN TERMINATED
HARD_WIDE.note: // Every keyword is a famous one-liner, shouted in capitals. Eight options below — tap the right one.
HARD_WIDE.weakHint: The catchphrases are the syntax. If you can hear the accent, you have the language.
HARD_WIDE.fact: ArnoldC (Lauri Hartikka) builds its entire keyword set from Arnold Schwarzenegger lines: IT'S SHOWTIME opens main, TALK TO THE HAND prints, and YOU HAVE BEEN TERMINATED ends it.

HARD_WIDE.note: // A complete program on a grid — the string is stored backwards and the pointer walks it out. Eight options below.
HARD_WIDE.weakHint: Look at the arrows: execution here changes direction instead of just reading on.
HARD_WIDE.fact: Befunge (Chris Pressey, 1993) is two-dimensional: > < ^ v steer the instruction pointer across the grid, the quoted string is pushed letter by letter, and @ ends the program. It was designed to be as hard as possible to compile.

HARD_WIDE.note: // A complete program in one line of backticks and dotted letters — each .x prints the character x. Eight options below.
HARD_WIDE.weakHint: Count the backticks and read the dotted letters one at a time — they spell the output in plain sight.
HARD_WIDE.fact: Unlambda is functional programming with the sugar removed: ` applies a function, and .x is a function that prints x. The greeting above is a chain of applications printing one character each.

HARD_WIDE.note: // A complete program: a rule, an empty rule that ends the list, and the seed string to rewrite. Eight options below.
HARD_WIDE.weakHint: Everything hangs on one very distinctive separator between a left side and a right side.
HARD_WIDE.fact: Thue (John Colagioia, 2000) executes by rewriting: rules a::=b replace text in the current string until nothing matches, and ~ in a replacement means "output this". It is Turing complete with no variables at all.

HARD_WIDE.note: // A complete program in eleven characters of string and one symbol. Eight options below.
HARD_WIDE.weakHint: The message is nearly the whole text — what matters is the single symbol that follows it.
HARD_WIDE.fact: FALSE (Wouter van Oortmerssen, 1993) is a stack language so terse that printing is one character: ß pops the string and writes it. Its Hello World fits in a headline.
